items.title: Jimmy Heath interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, September 8, 2014
items.q: I was remembering some of the things that Coltrane and Ornette Coleman did in the 60s.

ctx.x: Well the way I look at improvisation, you know you can step out of the basic chord pattern if you make the connections. In other words, life is about connections. Everything musically is about connections. Socially it’s about connections. Connections is one of the biggest words in the English language. You’ve got to make a connection. And that’s what I’m talking about. If you see, like I remember Theodore “Fats” Navarro. Great trumpeter. And Fats used to play — if a woman walked in with a red dress on [scats]…

Oh, that’s terrific. Sometimes when I think about the history of jazz it has moved so fast it seems like. And I was remembering some of the things that Coltrane and Ornette Coleman did in the 60s. And now that seems like, wow, what is that, 50 years ago. I wonder what your reaction was to records like “Ascension” and free jazz.

items.title: Jimmy Heath — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Then, the Japanese had just given Ornette Coleman $150,000.

ctx.x: Yeah (Laughs). I said the same thing that I’m saying on this microphone, “You’ve got to be kidding!” The Danish Jazzpar prize is $35,000, which I missed getting.

Tommy Flanagan got it; I was up for it. Then, the Japanese had just given Ornette Coleman $150,000. I went to one other thing where Ornette got Carnegie or something? Me and George Wein were sitting together and they gave him $200,00 or something, for another award. I’m saying to myself—and then my government is going to give me $20,00 and I’m supposed to scream, “Great! Great! I’m so happy!” What can I buy? I can buy a car and then I’m done. So I worked all my life for a car.
And then you didn’t get the car, and instead you composed a piece for a big band and made a recording.
